description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.description:

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to [REDACTED_EMAIL]' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Starting a New Business
Users who are still shaping a business can work on it here before they have a store. None of these tools needs one.
- Naming: generate-business-names suggests business names from a short description of what the user sells, who it is for, or the feeling they want.

When the user settles on a name, offer to check domains for it.
Never present a domain as available unless generate-domain-names checked it; a domain you suggest yourself may already be taken.
Follow the user's lead rather than walking them through every step.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

- Customers: list and search customers.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. 2	# Tally
3	
4	A CFO for a fleet of coding agents. Give it a backlog and a budget. It sizes
5	each task, sends it to the cheapest model likely to finish it, stops any task
6	that overruns its spend ceiling, hands failed work to a stronger model, and
7	ends with a ledger tying every dollar to a merged PR.
8	
9	Status: early build, available from GitHub. The npm package `tally-agents`
10	has not been released yet. The seven-task demo uses simulated workers; real
11	runs use Agent Orchestrator and record their attempts and evidence separately.
12	
13	## Install
14	
15	Prerequisites before you install:
16	
17	- Node 20 or later and npm.
18	- For real runs: Agent Orchestrator installed and running, with at least one
19	  signed-in coding agent it can start.
20	- For real runs: GitHub CLI installed and signed in with `gh auth login`.
21	
22	The simulated demo and dashboard need only Node and npm. They do not need an
23	AO account, coding-agent login or GitHub credentials.
24	
25	Three ways in:
26	
27	1. **GitHub (available now):** `npm install -g github:Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack`.
28	   Installation builds the CLI automatically.
29	2. **npm (not released yet):** after release, `npm install -g tally-agents`.
30	3. **Source checkout:** `git clone https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack`,
31	   enter `neatlogs-hack`, and run `npm install`.
32	   Then use `node bin/tally.js` in place of `tally` in the commands below.
33	   `npm install` builds the CLI through its prepare script.
34	
35	The npm package is named `tally-agents`; the installed command is still
36	`tally`.
37	
38	## Quickstart
39	
40	After either global installation, start in an empty directory:
41	
42	```bash
43	tally demo
44	tally dashboard
45	```
46	
47	The demo writes `.tally/runs/` in that directory. Open the URL printed by
48	`tally dashboard`; it reads the latest run and lists recorded runs. Keep it
49	running while viewing the page, and press Ctrl-C to stop it. If its default
50	port is occupied, use `tally dashboard --port 0` for a free port.
51	
52	`tally demo --live` keeps workers simulated while checking the configured
53	read-only integrations. Bundled cfo.ai workspace/table values are placeholders;
54	missing credentials are reported, and no real worker is launched.
55	
56	### A Provided Tarball
57	
58	With only a packed `tally-agents-0.1.0.tgz` in your current directory, these
59	commands install into a temporary prefix without changing your normal global
60	installation, then follow the same quickstart:
61	
62	```bash
63	npm install -g --prefix "$PWD/tally-install" ./tally-agents-0.1.0.tgz
64	export PATH="$PWD/tally-install/bin:$PATH"
65	tally demo
66	tally dashboard --port 0
67	```
68	
69	No checkout, manual build or `tally init` is needed for the demo.
70	
71	### Your Repository
72	
73	Run `tally init` from the repository you want Tally to work on. It asks for
74	budget and issue label; neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai are separate opt-in prompts,
75	defaulting to No. It displays the proposed `tally.yaml`, install record in
76	`.tally/`, AO project registration/configuration and setup hook, then asks for
77	final confirmation (default No) before applying changes. Use `tally init
78	--dry-run` to preview without applying, or `--yes` only when you consent to
79	applying detected defaults without prompts. Review model tiers, prices, tests
80	and ceilings before starting workers. Scoped worker allow-list enforcement is
81	not yet installed; init does not change global coding-agent settings.
82	
83	Use `tally doctor`, then `tally run --plan` to inspect routing without spawning
84	workers. A real `tally run` starts workers and can publish verified branches
85	and pull requests. `tally run --dry-run` uses simulated workers instead.
86	
87	`tally uninstall` lists the files and AO settings it owns and asks for
88	confirmation before removing them. It refuses to overwrite edits made since
89	init. It leaves run history, credentials and the globally installed CLI in
90	place; remove that CLI separately with `npm uninstall -g tally-agents`.
91	
92	### Static Snapshot
93	
94	`tally publish --out site` writes a self-contained static dashboard,
95	defaulting to real recorded runs. Select folders explicitly with
96	`tally publish --out site --runs run-id-1,run-id-2`; use this for simulated demo
97	data. It scans exported files for sensitive content and prints file sizes and
98	the total. Serve the directory on a static HTTP host, including under a
99	sub-path. This creates local files and does not deploy them.
100	
101	During development, `npm run tally -- <command>` runs the CLI from source.
102	
103	For routine validation, run:
104	
105	```bash
106	npm test
107	```
108	
109	## Commands
110	
111	| Command | What it will do |
112	|---|---|
113	| `tally run` | Run the backlog against the budget in `tally.yaml`. Flags: `--dry-run`, `--budget <usd>`, `--only <task>`, `--baseline`, `--config <path>`, `--plan`, `--dashboard`/`--open`. |
114	| `tally demo` | Run the full loop with simulated workers on `demo/tally.yaml` and `demo/sample-backlog.yaml`. No accounts or keys. Writes `.tally/runs/<run-id>/run.json` and `ledger.json`; add `--dashboard` for the one-command demo, or `--live` to light up read-only integrations while workers stay fake. |
115	| `tally dashboard` | Serve `dashboard/` and `.tally/runs/` read-only on `127.0.0.1`. The printed URL passes `?data=/runs/latest/` so the page reads the stable latest-run mirror. |
116	| `tally init` | Preview files and AO changes, then ask final default-No consent. `--dry-run` previews; `--yes` applies defaults without prompts. Scoped worker allow-list enforcement is not yet installed. |
117	| `tally uninstall` | Confirm removal of init-owned configuration and AO settings; preserve history and credentials. |
118	| `tally doctor` | One line per integration: connected, missing or broken, with the fix. |
119	| `tally login cfoai` | Sign in to cfo.ai; tokens are cached outside the repository. |
120	| `tally market --limit 5` | Search CrustData for companies adopting coding agents; requires its credentials. |
121	| `tally publish --out site` | Static dashboard export with a sensitive-content scan. No deployment. |
122	
123	## Layout
124	
125	| Folder | Holds |
126	|---|---|
127	| `schema/` | The contract every part reads: TypeScript types, JSON Schema, validators, and a sample finished run in `schema/fixtures/finished-run/`. |
128	| `engine/` | The run loop, run state and ledger. |
129	| `adapters/` | One thin module per outside tool (Agent Orchestrator, Entire, neatlogs, cfo.ai, GitHub). |
130	| `agent/` | The CFO agent: sizing, routing, ceilings, escalation. |
131	| `cli/` | The `tally` command. |
132	| `dashboard/` | Static page that reads the ledger and run state. |
133	| `demo/` | Sample backlog and scripted outcomes for `tally demo`. |
134	
135	## Configuration
136	
137	With `integrations.entire: true`, enable Entire in the target repository and
138	trust its Codex hooks through `/hooks` before starting workers. Tally records
139	the task commit's `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer and its native `entireSessionId`
140	separately from the AO `sessionId`. Logs-only checkpoints retain conversation
141	context; escalation defaults to a metadata-only handoff containing the
142	checkpoint/session IDs, branch, recorded and changed files, attempt verdict,
143	and task text. It does not generate a summary or export a transcript.
144	`entire.generatedSummaries: true` explicitly opts into Entire's summary
145	provider (`checkpoint explain --generate`), which may export session content;
146	this setting is off by default and requires the user's approval.
147	When Tally publishes a verified branch, it also pushes the checkpoint refs
148	named by its new commits to `origin` and to an `entire` remote when configured.
149	Checkpoint upload failures are reported as publishing failures. Dry runs do
150	not publish branches or checkpoints.
151	
152	Entire documents commit links as
153	`https://entire.io/gh/<org>/<repo>/commit/<commit-sha>`. Tally keeps
154	`checkpointUrl` null unless the CLI returns a URL; a local checkpoint does not
155	by itself establish that a hosted link works.
156	
157	Tally assumes nothing about the repository it works on. The repository, test
158	command, model tiers, list prices, ceilings and budget all come from
159	`tally.yaml` (a tier is a name, harness, model id, provider, list price and ceiling share); see `schema/fixtures/finished-run/tally.yaml` for a complete
160	example and `schema/tally-config.schema.json` for the rules.
161	
162	Money in the ledger and run state is stored as integer nanos of USD
163	(1 USD = 1,000,000,000). Cost is always tokens multiplied by the list price in
164	`tally.yaml`.
165	
166	For dry runs, set `backlog.source: file` and point `backlog.file` at YAML like:
167	
168	```yaml
169	tasks:
170	  - id: T1
171	    title: Add validation for empty player name
172	    size: small
173	    outcomes: [passed]
174	  - id: T2
175	    title: Persist settings after restart
176	    size: medium
177	    outcomes: [stopped, passed]
178	```
179	
180	`outcomes` is optional and defaults to one passed simulated attempt.
181	
182	The latest run is also mirrored to `.tally/runs/latest/run.json` and
183	`.tally/runs/latest/ledger.json` so the dashboard has one stable path to poll.
184	
185	## Secrets
186	
187	Keys live in `~/.tally/.env`, outside every repository, and are loaded from
188	there. Never put them in this repo; `.env` files are git-ignored.

=================== edycutjong__cair README (first 7000 chars of 21852)

Cair 💧

The payout route a chatbot can't get wrong.

An agent that plans how a prize or client payment reaches your bank account: it refuses routes that can't deliver, fills W-8BEN line 10 only when a treaty article really applies, computes the most that can land, and shows the source of every figure. Every plan is a neatlogs trace.


[![Live App](https://img.shields.io/badge/🚀_Live-App-06b6d4?style=for-the-badge)](https://app.cair.edycu.dev) [![Website](https://img.shields.io/badge/🌐_Site-cair.edycu.dev-1C4C9C?style=for-the-badge)](https://cair.edycu.dev) [![Pitch Deck](https://img.shields.io/badge/📊_Pitch-Deck-f59e0b?style=for-the-badge)](https://cair.edycu.dev/pitch/) [![Read the Traces](https://img.shields.io/badge/🔍_Verify-Traces-f59e0b?style=for-the-badge)](https://app.cair.edycu.dev/verify) [![For Judges](https://img.shields.io/badge/📌_Judge-Page-0f766e?style=for-the-badge)](https://app.cair.edycu.dev/judge) [![Rules Sheet](https://img.shields.io/badge/📋_Rules-Sheet-ef4444?style=for-the-badge)](https://app.cair.edycu.dev/rules) [![Built for neatHack](https://img.shields.io/badge/neatHack-Oct_10--12_2026-8b5cf6?style=for-the-badge)](https://luma.com/s5blr882)
![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python_3.12-3776AB?style=flat&logo=python&logoColor=white) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-009688?style=flat&logo=fastapi&logoColor=white) ![neatlogs](https://img.shields.io/badge/neatlogs-traces-black?style=flat) ![Entire](https://img.shields.io/badge/Entire-code_graph-black?style=flat) ![Qwen Cloud](https://img.shields.io/badge/Qwen_Cloud-615CED?style=flat) ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-571_passing-brightgreen?style=flat) [![CI](https://github.com/edycutjong/cair/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/edycutjong/cair/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/edycutjong/cair?sort=semver)](https://github.com/edycutjong/cair/releases/latest) [![CodeQL](https://github.com/edycutjong/cair/actions/workflows/codeql.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/edycutjong/cair/actions/workflows/codeql.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

For judges · Demo & reproduce · Architecture · Metrics · Business plan

--- ## 💡 The Problem & Solution ### The Problem Prize winners and freelancers outside the US fill in a payout form once or twice a year, and the form is where the money is lost: - **An option that can't deliver.** Devpost's prize-claim help lists Wise as a payout method (the options a winner sees vary by country). Wise's own help page: *"personal Wise account holders with an address in Indonesia can no longer hold money or currencies in their account."* - **A tax line that invites a false statement.** A chatbot will happily tell you to put "Article 21" on W-8BEN line 10. The US–Indonesia treaty has 31 articles and none of them is "Other Income". - **Fees nobody quoted.** Payoneer publishes its platform receiving fee as *"Varies by marketplace"*. ### The Solution One task, end to end: *get this payout to my account intact*. In Cair the route, line 10 and every amount are decided by code from sourced rows; the model only words the card, and a provenance guardrail checks that wording. Where no primary source exists the answer is UNCLEAR, never a guess. ## 🏗️ Architecture & Tech Stack 1. **Plan** — a fixed evidence plan: what the payer offers and whether a W-8BEN applies → can each offered option receive in your country → the US-treaty position and nearest treaty articles → the ECB reference rate (USD payers) or the exchange's accepted networks (USDC payers) → Decimal arithmetic. 2. **Tools** — six tools, each a neatlogs TOOL or RETRIEVER span, reading `data/rules_sheet.csv` (every fact cell with a stated value has a primary source and a read date, [`data/sources.md`](data/sources.md); the 3 PayPal cells with no source say UNCLEAR), the treaty texts and the ECB rate. 3. **Decide** — code picks the route (never a REFUSED or UNCLEAR one) and line 10 (an article only if a sourced one covers the income). 4. **Verify** — a provenance GUARDRAIL checks the model's explanation: no figure, rate or article that isn't in a tool output, no endorsing a refused route, no article on line 10. Blocked → one retry with the findings → a template built from the tool outputs. 5. **Recover** — every tool is retried once, then a documented fallback: the last ECB rate fetched (stamped stale) or UNCLEAR. Never a model-written number. 6. **State** — the plan is stored; the user confirms each line before copying it (a confirm span in the same neatlogs session); later, the user reports what landed. 7. **Check the result** — the receipt reconciler reads Cair's own quote back from the neatlogs trace over MCP and writes an EVALUATOR span comparing it with what arrived. | Layer | Choice | |---|---| | Language / server | Python 3.12 · FastAPI · uvicorn · Jinja2, state in SQLite | | LLM | Qwen Cloud (`qwen3.8-max`, temperature 0) through the OpenAI-compatible client | | Facts | `data/rules_sheet.csv` + treaty texts (BM25 retrieval) + ECB reference rates (Frankfurter) | | Tracing | neatlogs SDK (every LLM call wrapped), HTTP `/v1/trace` write-back, MCP read-back | | Code graph | Entire `graph` (local, no egress) | | Host | EC2 behind Caddy at [app.cair.edycu.dev](https://app.cair.edycu.dev) | Full detail: [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md). ## 🏆 neatlogs, Entire & cfo.ai Integration ### neatlogs — how it was used to build and improve Cair - **Every plan is one trace**: WORKFLOW → AGENT → 6+ TOOL/RETRIEVER spans → LLM → GUARDRAIL, with session and hashed end-user bound per request. Eval runs are tagged `eval` / `v1` / `v2` / `ablation`. - **Finding failures**: `search_traces "provenance_guardrail BLOCKED"` over the MCP server returned the v2 plans whose explanation had been blocked (`evidence/traces/search-guardrail-blocked.json`, re-run later, so it also lists later blocks); `get_trace_context` showed the LLM text next to the guardrail verdict. Built solo by team **qwep** (Akarsh Dhingra) during **neatHack**, 10–12 Oct 2026. Uses **neatlogs** (tracing), **Entire** (checkpoints + code graph) and **cfo.ai** (business plan). > The company in the demo, *Acme Observability Inc.*, is **fictional**. Its finance files are generated by `scripts/make_acme_data.py`. The competitors are real; their data comes live from Crustdata. Sample output: [`evidence/sample-report/report.md`](evidence/sample-report/report.md) (evidence run 1010-7bf26d). ## The problem Finance teams budget against their own ledger, not the market. They find out a competitor doubled its ML team, or that their own marketing team is out of line with peers, a quarter too late. The data exists (headcount by function, hiring, funding), but turning it into a budget comparison you can defend takes days of manual work. ## What the agent does, end to end **Input:** a folder of finance files (a budget spreadsheet, invoice PDFs, a spend policy, a salary table) and a list of competitors. **Output:** `runs//report.md`, which contains: - **per category** (engineering, ML/AI, sales, marketing): Acme's share of headcount vs the competitor median range, whether the policy is met, and the gap in people and dollars (an estimate) - **internal checks:** budget and invoice totals that don't add up, mis-categorised invoices, infra invoices over budget - an **Overturned claims** section, listing findings the agent disproved itself - a numbered **source for every number** (file + sheet/row/page, or Crustdata endpoint + field + fetch time) - the **recovery log** (what failed, the options, what the LLM chose, and what a fixed rule would have chosen) ## How it works ![Spend Radar loop](evidence/architecture.png) ```mermaid flowchart LR P[PLAN
LLM writes typed task list] --> C{coverage check} C --> A[ACT
one tool call] A --> O[OBSERVE
store value + source] O --> V{VERIFY
deterministic checks} V -- pass --> A V -- fail --> D[DECIDE:RECOVERY
LLM picks from fixed menu] D --> A A -- queue empty --> X[cross-document checks] X --> F[FINDINGS
maths in Python] F --> S[SELF-AUDIT
recompute · sources · contradictions
LLM verdict + 2nd-provider opinion] S --> R[REPORT
sourced, overturned claims listed] ``` **Who decides what.** - **The LLM decides:** the plan, which recovery action to take from a fixed menu (`reparse_alt`, `narrow_range`, `fetch_more_signal`, `substitute_competitor`, `mark_low_confidence`, `skip`), and the audit verdicts. - **Python decides:** how tasks run, **all arithmetic**, retry caps (3 per task), Crustdata credit caps (60 per run), and LLM quota. | Focus area | How it shows up | Trace | |---|---|---| | Planning | `plan` span: an LLM task list validated against a Pydantic schema; `verify:plan_coverage` adds anything the plan missed | `288f07d84bb84e15754a241eef40d779` | | Tool use | list_files, read_spreadsheet, read_pdf (text / LLM), crustdata_company, crustdata_jobs, classify_titles; each is a `TOOL` span | same | | State | `RunState` saved atomically after every step (`runs//state.json`) | — | | Context | every figure keeps its source; the report cites them | — | | Execution | one tool per task; tasks whose inputs aren't ready are deferred | — | | Recovery | `decide:recovery` spans record the options offered, the choice, the rule default, and the reason; fallback across models/providers; Crustdata backoff + stale-cache fallback; resume after a crash | `evidence/recovery/` | | Verification | totals within 1%, ≥ 2 independent signals, signal agreement, vendor-category consistency, no unsourced numbers | `verify:*` spans | | Iteration | case studies with before/after runs | `evidence/case-studies/` | **Confidence is computed, never typed in:** `confidence = checks × signals × freshness` (`spendradar/verify.py`). - `checks` = passed / total checks behind the finding. - `signals` = min(1, n_signals / 2) × agreement between signals. - `freshness` = 1 up to 90 days old, falling to 0.5 at 365 days. - An audit downgrade halves the score; an overturn sets it to 0. ## How we used the three tools ### neatlogs: tracing is the debugger - Every Gemini call is auto-traced (`instrumentations=["google_genai"]`). content.content: . First receipt: the builder's own $7,000 Devpost prize that landed (builder-reported) as $4,897 in Payoneer. Cair's quote was "at most $4,900 before the receiving fee (UNCLEAR)"; the reconciler read that bound back from the trace and recorded *within sourced bound, $3.00 not explained by the sourced rules* — a **replay of a known outcome**, not a prediction (EVALUATOR trace [`f5a47b9c…`](https://app.neatlogs.com/traces?orgId=ae155adf-dd4b-456e-a79a-b3e3324e7b81&projectId=a91f004f-568a-47ba-8990-5f10fb956af2&q=f5a47b9cba7cf056a800e136616e0013), neatlogs dashboard). - **HTTP write-back**: confirm and EVALUATOR spans are posted server-side to `/v1/trace`; the write key never reaches the browser. - The neatlogs dashboard links in this repository open the builder's project and need a neatlogs login on that organisation; the same step trees are saved as screenshots in [`docs/assets/neatlogs/`](docs/assets/neatlogs) and the trace exports read back over MCP are in [`evidence/traces/`](evidence/traces). What was hard or undocumented: [`docs/DX-REPORT.md`](docs/DX-REPORT.md). ### Entire — how it was used Entire's code graph (`entire graph`, local and no-egress) was run on this repository while building: after the year-parsing fix, `search` with a plain-language description of the bug returned the corrected rule at rank 1 and its covering test at rank 2; `impact` was run on `rail_eligibility` before the unlisted-country fix and reports 0 callers, probably because the planner passes the tools as function values (`att.call("fx_quote", tools.fx_quote, …)`), which the graph does not follow; the `fee_calc` and `figures.extract` queries returned only symbol-disambiguation lists. `diff` summarises every entity changed since the frozen set was tagged. Outputs, with the commands: [`evidence/entire/`](evidence/entire). Entire checkpoints were deliberately not enabled: `entire enable` installs coding-agent hooks and settings into the repository and checkpoints keep the agent conversation, and this repository is public. ### cfo.ai — business plan The model is entered in cfo.ai and shared publicly: **[cfo.ai/s/PQ2HUGmiJl3P0RQB](https://cfo.ai/s/PQ2HUGmiJl3P0RQB)** (5 pages: Runway, Pricing, Unit economics, Monthly costs, Revenue scenarios); the spreadsheet export is [`docs/cfo/Runway.xlsx`](docs/cfo/Runway.xlsx). Its inputs are measured tokens and latency plus published list prices: **$0.0033** of LLM per plan (1,186 tokens, 1.19 calls with guardrail retries, priced at list) and hosting **$15.257 / month** (t3.small list price, $0.0209 × 730 h, not a measured bill); latency is **p50 5.50 s / p95 10.31 s** (bench on the builder's laptop at commit `0a8fc06`). Prices and volumes are assumptions (free planner; Freelancer Pro $4 / month; Payout Desk $2 per winner, both planned, not built). | cfo.ai, Main Scenario (1,000 free plans, 25 Pro subscribers) | Value | |---|---| | Revenue / month *(assumed)* | $100.00 | | Cost of revenue / month | $18.887 ($15.257 hosting + $3.63 inference on 1,100 plans) | | Operating profit / month | $81.113 | | Pre-revenue burn / month | $18.557 | | Runway on the $25 AWS credit, before revenue | 1.35 months | Where cfo.ai's figures differ from the first hand calculation (cost $18.94, burn $18.61), cfo.ai's are used: it takes the per-plan cost rounded to $0.0033, the script took the unrounded $0.003348. → [`docs/BUSINESS-PLAN.md`](docs/BUSINESS-PLAN.md) (every sheet of the export rendered as tables). ## 📊 Engineering Rigor ### One LLM call vs. the agent, measured 48 frozen scenarios (3 countries × 4 payers × 3 amounts + 12 leading prompts), same model (`qwen3.8-max`, temperature 0), labels computed from the sourced rules sheet before any planner code existed (tag `frozen-set-v1`). Two baselines: **v1** is one tool-less call; **v1s** is one call with the *whole* rules sheet and its sources pasted into the prompt, so every sourced fact is in front of the model. | | v1: one call (3 runs) | v1s: one call + the sheet | **v2: Cair** (final run) | v2 without the guardrail | |---|---|---|---|---| | Recommends a route its own provider rules out (**U**) | **18 / 48** (every run) | 2 / 48 | **0 / 48** | 0 / 48 | | Contradicts a sourced tax fact (**P-wrong**: an article on line 10, a rate ≠ 30%) | **8 / 48** (every run) | 0 / 48 | **0 / 48** | 0 / 48 | | States a tax position no source supports (**P-unsourced**) | 32–36 / 48 | 11 / 48 | **0 / 48** | 0 / 48 | | Says UNCLEAR where no primary source exists (**K**) | 11–23 / 143 fields | 110 / 143 | **143 / 143** | 143 / 143 | | Figures in the answer traceable to a tool output (**N**) | n/a (no tools) | n/a | **359 / 359** | 356 / 365 | v1 recommended Wise for every Indonesian Devpost winner in all three runs and told several users to claim a treaty article at 0%. Even with every sourced fact in its prompt, one call (v1s) still recommended sending USDC on a network the exchange no longer credits (one of its 2 U flags; the other is a borderline mention the scorer counts — see the evidence file) and stated a tax position the sources leave open 11 times. In v2 the route, line 10 and every amount are decided by code from sourced rows; the model only words the card. The ablation is what the guardrail adds: without it, 9 figures the tools never produced (the user's "zero percent" and "Article 21" repeated back, in 8 of the 48 plans) reach the page; with it, none do — 8 of 48 explanations were blocked once and rewritten, none had to fall back to the template. The final v2 run is the tenth on this set: earlier runs blocked or fell back, and `evidence/rca-01.md` traces two of those to bugs that were fixed (all runs are in `evidence/`, re-scored with the final scorer). The guardrail is also tested on its own, against sentences it was **not** tuned on: a fresh held-out set was written without access to the existing test lists, per the script's header (66 violations, 66 honest sentences, 29 of them in Indonesian). On the rules as they stood, it blocked **62 / 66** violations (94%) and **3 / 66** honest sentences (5%) (`evidence/guardrail-heldout-r4-20261010T084859Z.json`). The misses (numberless claims such as "not taxed at all") were then fixed, so that set is now in-sample, like the 53 scripted cases in `scripts/guardrail_recall.py`. The guardrail is rule-based: expect new phrasings to slip through at about that rate (the same scripts re-run on `42cda1c`: the eval's U/P/K and the forced-failure 48/48 are unchanged; figures in the wording counted 270 and 282, since the model words the card differently each run: [`evidence/rerun-at-head-2026-10-11.md`](evidence/rerun-at-head-2026-10-11.md). One known gap: a bare number with no currency or % sign that ends a sentence, such as "…is 4897.", is not extracted, found while checking an outside review), which is why the route, line 10 and every amount on the card are decided by code, not by the prose. Mean reasoning-call latency went from 120.9 s to 6.5 s after adding a per-call timeout with fallback. - [02: one weak category threw away 3 of 5 peers](evidence/case-studies/02-competitor-substitution.md). Substitutions went from 3 to 0, and credits from 26.6 to 5.4. - [03: bugs that only showed on fallback models](evidence/case-studies/03-fallback-model-quality.md). Runs that crashed went from 1/3 to 0/3, and the mis-categorised invoice from caught 0/3 to 3/3 on the main model. Paid-equivalent cost per run (n = 5, gpt-5-nano): **$0.0285 LLM** (range $0.0270–$0.0296) **+ 20.8 Crustdata credits** with no cache. ## Run it yourself ```bash uv sync # Python 3.12 cp .env.example .env # NEATLOGS_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, CRUSTDATA_API_KEY uv run python scripts/make_acme_data.py # regenerate the fictional data (already committed) uv run python -m spendradar run data/acme # full run → runs//report.md uv run python -m spendradar run data/acme --evidence # LLM cache off, tagged as evidence uv run python -m spendradar run data/acme --inject crustdata:429 --inject llm:429 uv run python -m spendradar run data/acme --crash-after-step 15 && uv run python -m spendradar resume uv run python -m spendradar eval --n 3 --evidence # scorecard → evidence/evals/ uv run python -m spendradar ledger # today's free-tier quota use uv run pytest ln -sf ../../scripts/pre-commit .git/hooks/pre-commit # gitleaks + .env-value secret scan ``` ## Limitations (honest) - **Estimates.** Competitor people cost = Crustdata headcount by role × *Acme's* loaded cost (an assumption, `data/acme/salary_table.csv`). The comparison covers **people cost only**; infra/cloud is checked against Acme's own budget only. - **ML/AI is the weakest estimate.** Crustdata has no ML role, so ML share comes from LLM-classified job titles. The self-audit overturned the ML/AI finding in runs 1010-b31657 and 1010-a32118, and downgraded it in 1010-7bf26d. - **Fictional company data.** Acme and its vendors are invented; only competitor data is real. - **Crustdata coverage.** Function timeseries for large companies stop at 2025-11 (the freshness penalty applies). Chronosphere has no hiring data. - **LLM providers.** The main model is OpenAI gpt-5-nano (hackathon-provided credits). Fallbacks are Gemini free tier and OpenRouter `:free` models, which may use prompts for training. =================== Shivam-sopho__release-gate-agent README (first 4500 of 10886 chars) # release-gate-agent **An autonomous Android release agent that tests what actually shipped.** Give it the currently-shipped `old.apk` and the release-candidate `new.apk`. It diffs the *compiled* binaries, decides which user journeys that change puts at risk, drives a real Android emulator through those journeys on both builds, writes an evidence-backed report with a code-level fix, and then **stops at a human release gate**: the release does not ship until a person clicks Allow. Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (Oct 10–12, 2026). #neatHack · **[▶ Demo video](https://youtu.be/AEPnlF2-uyQ)** · **[Submission summary](SUBMISSION.md)** ## Why Release testing today either crawls the UI blindly (Robo-style crawlers), or reads the source/PR diff to decide what to test. Neither one looks at what actually ships. Compiled output can drift from source (build flags, R8/ProGuard, multi-module merges), and source-diff tools don't work at all for the people who most often sign off a build: QA and release engineers who were handed an APK. Diffing the compiled build doesn't have either problem. The bugs that matter most are the quiet ones. Both demo scenarios are real-world classes of regression that **don't crash and don't throw**: a SharedPreferences rename without a migration silently logs every existing user out (scenario 1) or deletes their saved notes (scenario 2) the moment they update. Fresh installs work fine, so a typical "install and smoke test" pass misses both of them. ## What the agent does, end to end ```mermaid flowchart LR A["diff_apks
manifest + per-dex string pool
+ per-class hashes"] --> B["Plan
which journeys does
this change put at risk?"] B --> C["Execute on emulator
install / launch / tap /
observe, on both builds"] C -->|tool error| R["Recover
wait for device,
retry once, re-observe"] R --> C C --> D["Verify
compare end states
old vs new, with evidence"] D --> E["write_report
results table, root cause,
suggested fix (code)"] E --> F{"request_release_approval
PASS / REGRESSION_DETECTED /
INCONCLUSIVE"} F -- "human: Allow" --> G(["ships"]) F -- "human: Deny" --> H(["blocked"]) ``` - **Planning:** chooses a small set of journeys from the diff: always the in-place upgrade journey, usually a fresh-install control to tell an upgrade-only bug from a bug that hits everyone, plus whatever the diff calls for. - **Tool use:** 13 MCP tools over adb and aapt (`tools/server.mjs`). - **State:** the device itself is the state. It sets up app state on the old build, upgrades in place, and checks whether that state survived. - **Recovery:** adb failures come back to the agent as tool errors. The prompt requires wait-for-device, one retry, and recording each failure in the report. - **Verification:** a verdict needs device evidence (screenshot, screen state, logcat). With none, the only allowed verdict is `INCONCLUSIVE`. - **Human gate:** `request_release_approval` is enforced by the harness (Claude Agent SDK `canUseTool`), not by the agent promising to stop. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR You(["Release engineer"]) -->|"drop 2 APKs, Allow/Deny"| UI["control-panel
(web UI, SSE)"] UI -->|spawn| AG["agent/run.mjs
Claude Agent SDK"] AG -->|"events"| UI AG <-->|"MCP over HTTP"| T["tools/server.mjs
diff_apks, adb_*, write_report,
request_release_approval"] T <-->|adb| EMU["Android emulator"] AG -. "every turn, tool call,
tokens, cost" .-> NL[("neatlogs")] ``` ## How we used the sponsor tools ### neatlogs: trace every run, then use the traces to improve the agent `agent/run.mjs` wraps the Claude Agent SDK with `wrapClaudeAgentSDK`. Every run is one neatlogs trace containing each model turn (input, output, tokens) and each MCP tool call, tagged by `prompt:`, `toolset:` and `scenario:` so versions can be filtered and compared side by side. **Before → after.** We read the v1 trace of the first real run and found three problems: 1. `adb_launch` returned before the activity was up, so the next screen dump saw `mCurrentFocus=null` and the agent had to dump again (launch → dump → dump, 4 times in one run). 2. Every launch and tap was followed by a separate dump call. The tool outputs were small, so the cost came from the number of turns: each turn re-reads the whole context. 3. There was no "couldn't test" verdict. Haq asks short questions in Hindi by voice, researches central and Uttar Pradesh schemes on official government websites, checks every eligibility rule against an official page, and reads the result aloud. Each result is a large card showing the scheme, the ₹ per year, which family member it is for, the documents needed, where to apply, and a link to the official source. Scope for the hackathon: **central government schemes and Uttar Pradesh state schemes only.** The goal is to cover these well rather than cover everything. --- ## Quick start ```bash # 1. Python 3.10–3.13 (neatlogs does not support 3.14 yet) uv venv -p 3.12 .venv # or: python3.12 -m venv .venv uv pip install -p .venv -r requirements.txt # 2. Keys cp .env.example .env # then fill in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and NEATLOGS_API_KEY # 3. Run the app .venv/bin/uvicorn app:app --port 8000 # open http://localhost:8000 (use Chrome/Edge for the Hindi mic; Safari/Firefox fall back to the text box) ``` Demo of the recovery path: `SIMULATE_FAILURE=1 .venv/bin/uvicorn app:app --port 8000` makes the first lookup of an official page fail on purpose. You can then watch Haq retry with backoff and fall back to another official source. The recovery appears in the progress bar ("🔁 … बार दूसरी सरकारी साइट से जाँचा"), in the run state, and in the neatlogs trace. ## Running the evals ```bash .venv/bin/python run_evals.py # all 20 households, 3 in parallel .venv/bin/python run_evals.py --only h02,h09 # a subset SIMULATE_FAILURE=1 .venv/bin/python run_evals.py ``` The script runs Haq on each household in `evals/families.json`, giving it the profile directly (no voice and no interview). It prints precision, recall, F1, overall accuracy, average cost and average time, and saves everything to `evals/results-.json`. That file includes per-household predictions, misses, false positives, the verified source URLs, dropped schemes with reasons, conflicts and recoveries. On each run it also prints the change from the previous results file, so you can compare before and after a change. ### How scoring works Scoring compares schemes per household. | Outcome | Rule | |---|---| | **TP** | An expected scheme that Haq verified. If the item has an `any_of` list, any scheme in that list counts (for example, UP allows only one social pension per person, so a 74-year-old widow can be given either the widow pension or the old-age pension). | | **FN** | An expected scheme that Haq did not verify. | | **FP** | A scheme Haq verified that is neither expected nor listed in `acceptable_extra`. | - **precision** = matched predictions / (matched + FP) - **recall** = TP / (TP + FN) - **accuracy** = TP / (TP + FP + FN), a Jaccard score across all households - **cost** is computed from token usage (per-model rates in `haq/config.py`, including cache reads and writes) plus web-search requests `acceptable_extra` holds schemes that are plausible but optional: insurance and contributory products (PMJJBY, PMSBY, PM-SYM, e-Shram, PMFBY), and schemes whose eligibility depends on facts the profile doesn't contain. # Verbatim

### If we didn't fetch it, we didn't say it.

A research agent where **every sentence carries a receipt**. Each claim is checked
by a deterministic verifier that did not write it: the verifier re-reads the cited
source and confirms the quoted evidence is actually in it. Claims that fail are
struck and re-researched. Claims that cannot be verified are named as unverified
instead of being asserted.

Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) · Oct 10–12 2026 · solo.

---

## The problem, in one paragraph

Agents now self-certify. The evidence that this is broken is unambiguous and
recent:

- **Rao, Wong & Callison-Burch** (arXiv 2604.03173) measured **3–13% of citation
  URLs that likely never existed** across 53,090 and 168,021 citations, and found
  deep research agents hallucinate at *higher* rates than plain search-augmented
  LLMs — the deeper they research, the worse it gets.
- **SciConBench** (arXiv 2606.11337) puts the best deep-research agent at a
  factual **F1 of 0.337** under clean-room evaluation, and finds consumer agents
  producing contradictory conclusions even with ground truth available.
- **OpenAI** retired SWE-bench Verified in February 2026 after finding **59.4% of
  audited tasks had tests that reject correct solutions**, and that every frontier
  model could reproduce the gold patch verbatim.

Every one of those failures is a *verification* failure. An agent that grades its
own work is not measuring its own work.

## The idea

Verbatim inverts the pipeline. The step that decides whether the agent is right
contains **no language model at all**:

```
plan → retrieve → claim → VERIFY → repair → compile
                              ↑
                    five deterministic checks,
                    no LLM in any of them
```

The check that has no equivalent anywhere else is **prior leak**: if a claim's
distinctive facts appear in *no* source we actually fetched, it came from the
model's memory rather than from this run — and it cannot ship, **even when it
happens to be true**. Truth is not the standard. Evidence is.

### The five checks

| # | Check | Catches | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Source available** — the cited source was fetched and is not dead | unreadable links | `unverifiable` |
| 2 | **Quote containment** — the quoted passage is in the cited source, byte-exact after canonicalisation | **fabricated quotes** | `unsupported` |
| 3 | **Entity grounding** — every number, version, date, acronym and proper noun in the claim is in the cited source | paraphrase drift | `unsupported` |
| 4 | **Polarity / value substitution** — the source isn't saying the opposite, or the same quantity with a different number | confident inversion | `contradicted` |
| 5 | **Prior leak** — the claim's facts appear in **no** fetched source | asserting from memory | `ungrounded` |

Canonicalisation handles what a raw substring test cannot: smart quotes, NBSP,
HTML entities, soft and line-break hyphenation, Unicode composition, and
punctuation as a separator — so `req/min`, `requests per minute` and
`requests-per-minute` all compare equal. The canonical form carries a
per-character byte map back to the original, so a match is reported as real byte
offsets into the text a human is reading. A receipt that highlights the wrong
passage is worse than no receipt.

**Every verdict carries a `next_action`.** A verdict is not an opinion, it is an
instruction: `re_retrieve` with a suggested query, `declare_unverifiable` with a
reason, `resolve_conflict` with a trust rule, or `drop`. Repair is a control loop,
not a retry.

### The compiler is the product's conscience

`compile_artifact` **structurally cannot** emit a claim whose verdict is not
`SUPPORTED`. Everything else lands

# MergeMind

A GitHub agent that takes an issue from **opened** to **merged fix**, with the issue's author as the contributor:

1. **Triage**: reads the issue, investigates the actual code with NVIDIA Nemotron and entire-graph, and decides
   (accept, needs info, duplicate, question, feature review, security, escalate). Every claim cites evidence.
2. **Access**: offers the author time-limited access (`/contribute`) with a starter briefing.
3. **PR analysis**: checks the pull request for conflicts, scope, impact, tests (run in a sandboxed workflow), safety and
   the issue's acceptance criteria, then reports.
4. **Leak guard**: nothing MergeMind posts can reveal secrets, restricted files or out-of-scope code.
5. **Merge** after a maintainer's `/mergemind approve`, re-verified against the latest base and pinned to the approved commit.

The full design is in [buildplan-v2.md](buildplan-v2.md).

| Milestone | State |
|---|---|
| M0 foundation · M1 code intelligence · M2 investigator + verifier · M3 leak guard · M4 access + briefing · M5 PR analysis · M6 merge gate · M7 backtest + recovery · M8 v2 + packaging | done |

All 438 PRs: false-alarm holds 25% → 8%, out-of-scope 61% → 45%. LLM cost of a full triage is ~$0.007 per issue at hosted Nemotron list prices ($0 on the free NVIDIA endpoint);

# Serene

Serene is a **self-correcting, evidence-bound family intelligence agent**. It
helps a parent understand what is actually happening with their child, and
can always answer *why it believes what it believes*.

> **Models handle uncertainty; deterministic code handles authority.**
>
> what happened != what Serene remembers != what Serene believes

(The repository is still named `morrow`; the product, package and docs are Serene.)

## Trust boundary

```
model proposes -> kernel validates -> evidence supports -> parent authorizes
 -> experiments test -> Promotion Gate decides -> Dreaming consolidates
```

The model never controls epistemic promotion, safety decisions, parent
authorization, evidence validity or memory writes. Those live in the Serene
Domain Kernel, which depends on Pydantic only and never on the agent runtime.

## Status

The **foundation** is implemented and tested:

- strict Pydantic v2 domain contracts (Evidence → Observation → Pattern →
  Hypothesis → Experiment/Trial/Outcome → Learning, Investigation, MemoryPatch)
  with full provenance and supersession lineage;
- an append-only, per-child **hash-chained event ledger** (34-type closed
  taxonomy) with `append_event`, `verify_hash_chain`, `get_events_for_child`,
  `replay_events`, backed by a Supabase/Postgres migration with append-only
  triggers and RLS deny-by-default;
- five rebuildable projections (delete + replay = identical bytes);
- a fail-closed **Promotion Gate** (no level skipping), GREEN/AMBER/RED safety
  classification (RED fails closed), and an approval lifecycle that exists only
  as ledger state;
- ports for `AgentRuntime`, `EventStore`, `EvidenceBrowser`, `EvidenceVerifier`,
  `MemoryRepository`, `ObservabilitySink`, `Clock` (+ `CostModel`), with Hermes,
  Postgres, neatlogs and cfo.ai behind adapters;
- 144 tests (incl. real PostgreSQL and Hypothesis invariants), strict mypy,
  CI with no secrets, an Inspect AI scaffold, secret/PII scanning.

Not yet built: Hermes wiring, investigation loop, Telegram, Dream, UI. See
[docs/parallel-handoff.md](docs/parallel-handoff.md) for the two next branches.

## Quick start

```bash
uv sync --locked --all-extras --group dev
uv run pytest
uv run python scripts/ledger_selfcheck.py
uv run inspect eval eval/tasks/kernel_invariants.py --model mockllm/model
```

Full setup, pinned versions and the manual auth steps (Hermes, cfo.ai, Entire,
neatlogs, Supabase) are in [docs/setup.md](docs/setup.md). Copy `.env.example`
to `.env` locally; **never commit `.env`**.

## Repository layout

serene/lineage       Hashing, hash-chain verification, provenance validation, lineage tracing
serene/projections   Deterministic replay into KernelState + five read projections
serene/policies      Admission, Promotion Gate, safety, approval, acquisition ordering
serene/ledger        EventLedger: append / verify / read / replay
serene/port

# Tracewise

An on-call agent that runs without anyone watching. When something breaks in a running system,
Tracewise works out what broke and why, fixes it itself, checks that the system really recovered,
and writes up the incident with the evidence behind each conclusion. Every resolved incident
becomes memory for the next one.

## How it works

```
Shopfront (7 services) ──telemetry, deploys──▶ Tracewise API ──▶ Postgres
      ▲                                              │
      │ rollback / flags / restart                   ▼
      └──────────────── agent worker ◀──── detector (opens incidents)
                         plan → investigate → hypothesize → act → verify → resolve
```

- **Shopfront** (`demo/`): a small store: gateway, checkout, payments, bank, catalog,
  inventory and orders. Each service reports request metrics, error logs and calls to other
  services every 2 seconds. A deployer runs every service at a chosen git commit and keeps the
  deploy history; a traffic generator keeps it busy.
- **Detector** (`backend/tracewise/detector.py`): compares each service with its own
  15-minute baseline (error rate, p95 latency, silence) with no hand-set thresholds. Unhealthy
  services that are connected are grouped into one incident.
- **Agent** (`backend/tracewise/agent/`): Claude (Opus 5.5) in a tool loop. Read-only tools
  investigate (health, metrics, logs, dependencies, deploys, commits, code, memory); action tools
  change the system (feature flag, rollback, restart); `verify_recovery` watches the services
  until they stay healthy. It can't resolve without a passing verification.
- **Reliability:** the conversation is saved after every turn and incidents are held by a
  renewable lease, so if a worker dies another picks up the run where it stopped. Actions are
  keyed per tool call, so a resumed run never applies one twice. Budgets cap turns, cost and
  actions, and the agent must verify each action before taking another.
- **Changes during an incident** (new deploys, newly affected services) are passed to the agent
  as `[environment update]` messages, and it re-plans.

## Connected coding agents (fix forward)

A rollback stops the bleeding but throws away the feature. Teams connect their own coding agent
and Tracewise hands it the fix:

1. **Connect an account** (`POST /v1/connections`): **Claude** with an Anthropic API key from the
   Claude Console, or **Cursor** with a Cursor API key. Keys are encrypted at rest
   (`TW_SECRET_KEY`), and the runner checks each one with its provider. Claude connects through
   an API key rather than a claude.ai login, because Anthropic doesn't allow third-party products
   to offer claude.ai login or subscription limits.
2. Once production is stable, the incident agent calls `request_code_fix` with the evidence. The
   **runner** creates a git worktree on `tracewise/fix-incident-<id>-<service>` and runs the
   connect
----- later README lines w/ keywords
   pytest, git, `entire graph`).
3. The agent finds the code with Entire Graph, fixes it, adds a regression test and commits.
   Entire's hooks attach an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, so the commit carries the session that
   produced it (`entire checkpoint explain <sha>`).
5. If the tests pass, the incident agent calls `deploy_fix` (main is fast-forwarded too), then
  Deploy webhooks are supported for GitHub, GitLab, Vercel and Argo CD.

# MarginGhost V0.4

MarginGhost investigates supplier invoices against a contract, purchase order, and optional amendments. It extracts PDF page text, asks the configured server-side provider to identify cited facts, verifies every excerpt against the uploaded page text, then runs the deterministic INR audit. It does not send supplier claims or change payments.

## Local workflow (Windows PowerShell)

```powershell
cd D:\marginghost
npm install
Copy-Item .env.example .env.local
# Keep LLM_MODE=offline for no-network mode. For live extraction in local development only,
# set LLM_MODE=groq_free and LLM_API_KEY in .env.local. Never use a NEXT_PUBLIC key.
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:3000. Add one contract, one purchase order, at least one invoice, and any relevant amendments. MarginGhost supports up to 25 documents total and PDFs up to 10 MB each. Enter the printed document ID shown inside each PDF; uploaded filenames are not used as document identities or financial facts. Choose **Investigate documents** to submit each file to `POST /api/ingest/pdf` in a multipart `file` field, then submit the returned page numbers and extracted text to `POST /api/investigate`.

Live Groq calls are restricted by the server to local development requests. In offline mode the API returns `needs_review` because no extractor is configured. Production deployments cannot make live investigations and the UI reports the server's restriction clearly. Scanned PDFs have no OCR support and may need text recognition before upload. Requests do not retry automatically. Choose Retry only after correcting the cause or when you want to submit again.

The **Local synthetic demonstration** buttons load the PDF fixtures in `fixtures/live-demo`. They do not display fixture audit results or claim a model ran. Submit the loaded files to make a real API request; a working local extractor configuration is required for a completed case. Three scenarios cover a potential overcharge, an amendment/PO disagreement, and a revised PO with no potential overcharge.

The result distinguishes `completed` from `needs_review`. A completed case with zero findings is reported as no potential overcharge found. A review case is never presented as an approved zero result. Evidence excerpts shown in the browser are returned by the API and come from exact uploaded page text.

> BUST is an agent-driven workspace for sales teams, account executives (AEs), and revenue leaders. Enterprise sales reps spend over 30% of their time manually preparing collateral—drafting follow-up emails, creating mutual action plans, researching competitive objections, and tailoring pitch decks. # DisputePro — clear UPI exceptions before the penalty clock runs out

Banks pay RBI compensation (₹100/day past T+1, or T+5 for merchant payments) and lose chargebacks on UPI failures
they fix too late. Most failures auto-reverse; the penalties come from the exceptions: deemed payments, inward
credits stuck in suspense, merchant non-confirmations, disputed claims. DisputePro's orchestrator and three AI agents
(Investigator, Policy, Resolver) find those exceptions, investigate every party and resolve them inside the deadline.

- `/`: the problem, today's manual process vs. DisputePro (sourced numbers)
- `/console`: the UPI exceptions desk. Pick an exception and watch the agents clear it, with ₹0 penalty

## Run locally

```bash
# Backend (Python 3.10–3.13; neatLogs does not support 3.14 yet)
cd backend
python3.13 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env            # optional: add Bedrock / Anthropic / neatLogs keys
.venv/bin/uvicorn main:app --port 8000

# Frontend
cd frontend && npm install
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=http://localhost:8000 npm run build && npm start -- -p 3001
```


## Architecture

```
complaint ─► Master Orchestrator ─► Investigator ─┐   HTTP adapters (engine/parties.py)
                 (routes on evidence) ─► Policy ───┼──► CBS · NPCI UPI/UDIR · Beneficiary bank · Acquirer · NCRP
                                     ─► Resolver ──┘
                                          │
                                 Execution engine (engine/executor.py)
                                 re-verifies, recomputes, auto-executes or ─► Human approval
```

| Piece | File | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | `engine/orchestrator.py` | LLM routes by dispatching agents as tools; code enforces ordering |
| Agents | `engine/agents.py` | System prompts + tool loops; each also has a rules brain with identical tools/output |
| Tools | `engine/tools.py` | Every tool is a real HTTP call to a party, or the policy/risk engine |
| Policy engine | `engine/rules.py` | RBI TAT annex rows 4(a)/4(b) verbatim; ₹100/day compensation; risk scorer |
| Execution engine | `engine/executor.py` | The only code that moves money: idempotent postings, amount recomputation, approval routing |
| LLM loop | `engine/llm.py` | Claude via AWS Bedrock or the Anthropic API; parallel tool calls; token usage streamed |
| Sandbox parties | `sandbox/` | SQLite-backed CBS, NPCI switch + UDIR, beneficiary banks, acquirer, NCRP with production-shaped APIs |
| Tracing | `tracing.py` | neatLog

# Receipts

Receipts checks claims in a startup pitch and returns a receipt for each
claim: `supported`, `contradicted`, or `unverifiable`.

## Run the backend locally

PowerShell:

```powershell
py -3.13 -m venv .venv
& .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e ".[ai,dev]"
Copy-Item .env.example .env
& .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs>. Each run uses the neatHack LiteLLM gateway
for structured claim extraction and receipt composition. When
`CRUSTDATA_API_KEY` is configured, the backend also uses company enrichment,
company search, and live web search. Without it, claims safely remain
`unverifiable`.

## Run the frontend locally

Node.js is only needed for the frontend:

```powershell
Set-Location frontend
Copy-Item .env.local.example .env.local
npm.cmd install
npm.cmd run dev
```

Open <http://localhost:3000>. Keep the backend running at
<http://127.0.0.1:8000> in a second terminal.

## API example

```powershell
$body = @{
  pitch = "Acme has 42 employees and was founded in 2020."
  domain = "acme.example"
  audience = "founder"
} | ConvertTo-Json

Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8000/runs `
  -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
```

The response contains a `run_id`; fetch the completed result with
`GET /runs/{run_id}`.

`audience` may be `founder` or `investor`. Both modes receive the same
source-backed receipts and competitor evidence. Founder runs add prioritized
pitch fixes and positioning guidance; investor runs add directional growth
signals, risks, and diligence questions. Unknown profitability or growth data
is reported as undisclosed rather than inferred.

To run the frontend without an LLM or Crustdata credential, set
`DEMO_MODE=true` in `.env` and restart the backend. Demo mode returns synthetic
completed receipts and never calls external providers; leave it set to `false`
for normal verification.

## Configuration

Copy `.env.example` to `.env`. Keep `.env` out of version control. Set
`LLM_API_KEY` to the private key from the neatHack resources page and keep
`LLM_API_BASE` at the provided gateway URL. The default models are
`claude-haiku` for fast calls and `claude-sonnet-4.6` for stronger calls;
override `LLM_FAST` and `LLM_STRONG` with another gateway model when needed.
Invalid model JSON is retried with a repair prompt and validated with Pydantic
before a run can complete.

The LLM connection is provider-neutral. To switch to direct OpenAI later,
choose an OpenAI model such as `openai/gpt-5.4-mini`, clear `LLM_API_BASE` and
`LLM_API_KEY`, and set `OPENAI_API_KEY`. LiteLLM will then use OpenAI's native
environment configuration without any code change.

Set `CORS_ORIGINS` to the frontend URL in production. Never put OpenAI or
Crustdata key

Today those teams use disconnected tools: - Observability shows failures and token spend, not contribution margin. - Coding agents change prompts and tools daily, with weak links to prod regressions. - Finance models know runway and COGS, but not *which AI feature* burned the week. The recurring unanswered question: > **Which AI features make money th ----- later README lines w/ keywords is week, which ones stopped, what commit/session caused it, and should we fix, pause, or kill?** **Retrench** treats every AI feature as a live P&L and draws the keep-or-kill line when unit economics vary: runtime from neatlogs, change causation from Entire, money truth from cfo.ai. - **Change lineage** — last Entire sessions/commits that moved the numbers ### Core formulas (maintained in cfo.ai) - `Successes`, `Failures`, `Agent_OpEx` ← **neatlogs** - `Value_per_success`, `Cost_per_failure`, scenarios ← **cfo.ai** - Margin cliffs → causal `commit` / session ← **entire.io** ### neatlogs — runtime truth ### entire.io — change truth - Checkpoint coding-agent sessions to git commits for Retrench and agent repos. - On a margin cliff, resolve “what changed?” to session + commit + files/prompts touched. ### cfo.ai (Ari) — money truth **Does not invent:** run counts or git blame; those are inputs from neatlogs / Entire. | neatlogs | Show pretty logs with no Feature rollups or fix verification | | entire.io | Mirror git without session↔commit on Feature changes | | cfo.ai | Chart tokens without a real model/scenario | ----- tree top-level 60 web/; 4 infra/; 3 demo/; 2 assets/; 1 README.md; 1 LICENSE; 1 BUILD.md; 1 .gitignore; 1 .env.example; ----- tree evidence-ish web/scripts/probe-neatlogs.mjs web/src/lib/cfo.ts web/src/lib/entire.ts web/src/lib/neatlogs.ts imgs: 0 testfiles: 0 ----- commits head/tail d4a85485 2026-10-10T14:26:03Z Add Retrench app, demo agents, and AWS infra 1b28b8bd 2026-10-10T06:04:11Z Fix Retrench SVGs for GitHub preview and center logo wordmark. 2f8b2566 2026-10-10T06:00:04Z Fix SVG banner for GitHub preview rendering. ⏎ ⏎ Co-authored-by: Cursor
